Thomas Hunt Morgan. The American biologist and embryologist who founded experimental genetics through his work with Drosophila melanogaster, the common fruit fly. His discoveries proved that genes had physical locations and obeyed Mendelian laws, transforming biology from descriptive to experimental.

Morgan discovered sex-linked inheritance through the white-eye mutation in fruit flies. This trait was inherited in a pattern tied to the X chromosome, and this observation proved that genes resided on chromosomes, not just as abstract hereditary units. He established the fruit fly as the model organism for genetics. Flies were cheap, short-lived, thousands of mutants were available, and they were amenable to precise breeding and counting. This practical choice multiplied the power of his experiments.

Morgan developed genetic mapping, the concept that genes occupy linear positions on chromosomes measurable by recombination frequency. This gave genetics a quantitative framework. He created the Caltech School of Biology, and his fly lab became a world centre for genetics, attracting researchers from everywhere. He demonstrated that mutations were heritable, non-random changes in genes, not spontaneous reversions or environmental effects. He introduced the term gene as the hereditary unit itself, unifying Mendelism with cytology.

In 1933, Morgan won the Nobel Prize for this work. Barbara McClintock would later extend his genetic theories by discovering transposable elements, while James Watson and Francis Crick would reveal the physical structure of the genes that Morgan's work had mapped genetically.
